files.author: Diego Delso
files.description: Young male of common eland (Taurotragus oryx), Masai Mara, Kenya. This large savannah and plains antelope is found in East and Southern Africa. An adult male is around 1.6 m (5.2 ft) tall at the shoulder and can weigh up to 942 kg (2,077 lb) with a typical range of 500–600 kg (1,100–1,300 lb). It is the second-largest antelope in the world, being slightly smaller on average than the giant eland. Mainly a herbivore, its diet is primarily grasses and leaves.

files.fileTitle: File:The Juliana’s golden mole is one of Africa’s most threatened mammals Jackson.png
files.author: Photograph by Craig R. Jackson, CC BY 4.0.
files.description: Original description, according to the source, p. 76: "Figure 3.C (Top) The Juliana’s golden mole is one of Africa’s most threatened mammals. Photograph by Craig R. Jackson, CC BY 4.0. [...]" Context in the source, page 74f: "To remedy the dearth in knowledge on two endemic South African golden mole species, we analysed molecular data of individuals collected across the entire distribution range of both Juliana’s golden mole (Neamblysomus julianae, EN) and Hottentot golden mole (Amblysomus hottentotus, LC) (Figure 3.B). In contrast to the widespread Hottentot golden mole, the Juliana’s golden mole counts among South Africa’s most imperilled mammals and is known from only three range-restricted, geographically isolated populations (Maree, 2015, Maree et al., 2016; Maree, 2017; Taylor et al., 2018). These three populations, together covering less than 160 km2 occur in southeastern Pretoria (Gauteng population), the district of Modimolle (Limpopo, ~ 120 km north of Pretoria), and in southwestern Kruger National Park (Mpumalanga, ~ 400 km east of Pretoria) (Figure 3.C)."

files.fileTitle: File:African palm swifts (Cypsiurus parvus) showing them around their palm (Hyphaene petersiana) habitat. - 52735043332.jpg
files.author: Derek Keats
files.description: Something I have been trying to get to work for years, photos of African palm swifts (Cypsiurus parvus) that show them around their palm (Hyphaene petersiana) habitat. This species is found over most of sub-Saharan Africa, and is very common in South Africa. I took these yesterday, in the parking lot at Babalala Picnic site north of Shingwedzi Rest Camp in Kruger National Park. The wind direction meant that they slowed a bit as they passed the trees, and I was able to capture some images showing the palm leaves in the background.
